title: Opening the Peer Review Process
text:
Peer review remains the principal mechanism through which academic journals assess the validity of submitted research. Before a manuscript is accepted, it is typically evaluated by two or three independent experts who scrutinise its methodology, statistical rigour, and interpretation of results. Although this process is widely regarded as essential, it has been criticised for being slow and, at times, inconsistent across disciplines. Reviewers are usually anonymous, a practice intended to encourage candid feedback but which has also drawn scrutiny for allowing biases to go unchecked.

In response to these concerns, some journals have experimented with open peer review, in which the reviewers' identities and their comments are published alongside the article. Proponents argue that this transparency discourages careless criticism and makes the evaluation process easier to audit. Critics, however, worry that reviewers may become reluctant to point out serious flaws when their names are attached to the report. Early evidence suggests that the effects vary considerably depending on the field and the culture of the journal involved.

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what do proponents of open peer review argue?
options: That it makes articles longer to write
That editors should choose the reviewers
That reviewers should be paid for their work

questions.text: What can be inferred about the critics' main concern regarding open peer review?
options: Reviewers might soften their criticism when their names are attached.
The process takes too long to be useful.
Journals should stop publishing research altogether.
Editors ignore comments made by reviewers.

questions.text: What does the author imply about the effects of open peer review?
options: They will be identical in every academic field.
They may depend on the discipline and the journal's culture.
They have already proven that open review is superior.
They are too small to affect publishing decisions.

paragraph_translations: La revisión por pares sigue siendo el principal mecanismo mediante el cual las revistas académicas evalúan la validez de las investigaciones presentadas. Antes de aceptar un manuscrito, normalmente lo evalúan dos o tres expertos independientes, que examinan su metodología, su rigor estadístico y la interpretación de los resultados. Aunque este proceso se considera esencial, se le ha criticado por ser lento y, en ocasiones, poco consistente entre disciplinas. Los revisores suelen ser anónimos, una práctica pensada para fomentar comentarios sinceros, pero que también ha sido cuestionada por permitir que los sesgos pasen desapercibidos.

Como respuesta a estas preocupaciones, algunas revistas han experimentado con la revisión abierta por pares, en la que las identidades de los revisores y sus comentarios se publican junto con el artículo. Quienes la defienden sostienen que esta transparencia desalienta las críticas descuidadas y facilita la auditoría del proceso de evaluación. Los críticos, en cambio, temen que los revisores se muestren reacios a señalar fallos graves cuando su nombre aparece en el informe. Las primeras evidencias sugieren que los efectos varían considerablemente según el campo y la cultura de la revista involucrada.
